lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on borders, near and far
lead.head: Where the map ends, chai begins

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 51

play.label: Hear the case, and the catch

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah recorded this episode out­doors, in a place that could have been any­where. That, Varma said, was the point: “You don’t need to look at lines on maps.”
The food writer Pushpesh Pant, he re­called, car­ries other maps in his head, drawn for in­stance by which sour­ing agent a re­gion uses: tamarind or kokum, jack­fruit or lime. {051-S01}

Yet in ge­og­ra­phy class we are handed po­lit­i­cal maps and told who we are, and that the other per­son is a for­eigner. Varma ar­gued that these frames, ab­sorbed with­out our notic­ing, hold us back.
The hosts made the case that such lines are un­nat­u­ral to the way peo­ple live. Then Shah of­fered the case against.
## Gravity, bor­rowed

Shah began with eco­nom­ics. Trade be­tween two coun­tries, econ­o­mists found, is roughly pro­por­tional to their GDPs mul­ti­plied to­gether and di­vided by the square of the dis­tance be­tween them: a “grav­ity model” echo­ing Newton.
Shah stretched it to all human af­fairs. “What peo­ple do with each other is in­versely pro­por­tional to the dis­tance squared,” he said. {051-C01}
Then he zoomed into a bor­der, such as the one be­tween East and West Bengal. It is not a de­mil­i­tarised zone out of a John le Carré novel, he said, but a field, with a house on each side.

The two fam­i­lies talk, party at night, marry and do busi­ness with each other, and their chil­dren play to­gether. Fence the field, and the per­son at the cen­tre of that cir­cle loses half their so­cial net­work.
“So you’ve taken the small­est unit of that tribe and you’ve put a line through their heart,” Shah said. {051-C02}
## The ab­stract and the con­crete

For Varma the line on the map is an ab­strac­tion. The con­crete re­al­ity is peo­ple eat­ing, drink­ing, mar­ry­ing and being friends. “We are to­gether on the din­ner table when we have biryani and raita,” he said. {051-C03}

Europe, Shah said, shows what can be done. Germany in­vaded France in 1870, in 1914 and in 1940. Today peo­ple live in France, drive to jobs in Germany and carry no pa­pers across a bor­der with no check­points. He called it “the height of civ­i­liza­tion”.

Varma in­voked the philoso­pher W. E. H. Lecky’s ex­pand­ing cir­cle of moral con­cern, from fam­ily to tribe to na­tion to all hu­man­ity. It can­not be taken for granted, he warned, and lines on maps stand in its way.
Technology has helped. The in­ter­net, Varma said, let him move “from com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance to com­mu­ni­ties of choice”. {051-C10}
## The catch
Shah of­fered two cau­tions. Distance has died only for elec­trons: pots of honey and rice are heavy, and peo­ple still need to meet, share chai and touch.

And a bor­der can break a peo­ple if the state goes all the way, with elec­tri­fied fences, dogs and ma­chine guns kept up for fifty or sev­enty-five years. North and South Koreans, he said, can now barely speak to each other.
Varma wor­ried about walls built of words, rhetoric that splits neigh­bours liv­ing side by side. They grow sharper, he ar­gued, where there is scarcity, no mar­kets and an op­pres­sive state.
His clos­ing rec­om­men­da­tion fit­ted the theme: Agota Kristof’s *The Notebook Trilogy*, set in a bor­der­land where sol­diers come and go and chil­dren try to make sense of the world.

second.label: The Texas border
second.head: Next door is Mexico
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why the nation fades as you near the border

pic.caption: A fence separates Tijuana, Mexico, from the United States near San Diego, 2007
pic.credit: Sgt. 1st Class Gordon Hyde, public domain

body: Ajay Shah said the idea for this episode came alive while he read human sto­ries from the Texas–Mexico bor­der. One in­ter­view was with a per­son in a town 300 me­tres from a Mexican city. {#mexico}
For that per­son, the peo­ple across the line were friends and neigh­bours. Far away, the de­bate was about two coun­tries and keep­ing mi­grants out. Up close, life fol­lowed the grav­ity law.

The na­tion, Shah said, is an imag­ined com­mu­nity, fic­tional be­cause it is so far away. “Whereas the re­al­ity is the bloke that I meet when I wake up in the morn­ing and who do I have chai with?” {051-S03}

quote.text: at the lived re­al­ity, you are with your peo­ple, and your peo­ple are the peo­ple near you.

third.head: How one people became two

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on keeping a people apart

body: Ajay Shah then ar­gued against him­self. Build the elec­tri­fied fence, add dogs and elec­tric eyes, keep it up for fifty or sev­enty-five years, and you can break the one­ness of a peo­ple. {#oneness}

North and South Koreans today are barely able to speak to each other, he said. One is a des­per­ately poor coun­try, the other an ad­vanced OECD econ­omy, and the North does not know what to do with K-pop. {#korea}

When the Berlin Wall came down in 1989, Germans had not moved freely since 1945, and those raised in the East, it is said, still carry psy­chic wounds. Shah’s rule: “if you will keep the peo­ple apart for enough gen­er­a­tions, then they will grow apart.” {051-C12}
He added: “Not that I’m rec­om­mend­ing this to any­body who’s watch­ing the show.” {051-J05}

p2.title: The lie of the land
p2.deck: From the gravity model to the Berlin Wall, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take apart the border, chapter by chapter

from1.head: Where the map ends, chai begins

quote.text: Borders in the real world are just that there is a field and by dumb luck some line hap­pens here.

box.title: Maps the state didn’t draw
box.text: Amit Varma pointed to Arati Kumar-Rao’s work on people’s lived con­nec­tion with the land, a con­trast to the maps of ge­og­ra­phy class. Pushpesh Pant, he re­called, car­ries imag­ined maps drawn by sour­ing agent: tamarind or kokum, jack­fruit or lime. {051-S01}

sections.label: The first law
sections.head: The pull of the neighbour
sections.caption: the gravity model of human interaction
body: Ajay Shah opened with a para­ble. The Lord held an ac­count­abil­ity ses­sion and asked each pro­fes­sion to show it had added value. Among the economists’ claims was the grav­ity model. “Gravity?” said the Lord. “But that’s what the physi­cists do.” {051-J01}
Economists, Shah ex­plained, found that trade be­tween two coun­tries is pro­por­tional to the prod­uct of their GDPs di­vided by the dis­tance be­tween them squared.

Distance must be read broadly: two English-speaking coun­tries are ef­fec­tively closer than an an­glo­phone and a fran­co­phone one. Then the econ­o­mists, “being im­pe­ri­al­ists”, gen­er­alised the law: move two peo­ple from 10 kilo­me­tres apart to 20, and their in­ter­ac­tion falls by four times, not two. {#fourx}
## Floors apart

This is the logic of the dense city, Shah said. He claimed that even the num­ber of floors be­tween neigh­bours, the sec­onds of a lift ride, changes how often they meet. Amit Varma of­fered his own build­ing: its sec­re­tary is a fa­mous as­trologer, ap­par­ently, and Varma does not know which floor he lives on. {051-J02}
Applied to a bor­der, the law is cruel. By the time you are fifty or sixty kilo­me­tres away, Shah said, the line barely mat­ters; at the bor­der it­self, half your world is cut away. {#sixtykm}
~ Shah had con­fessed to physics envy. Varma said he was rather an econ­o­mist “who has a poet’s heart”. {051-J03}

quote.text: Borders in the real world are just that there is a field and by dumb luck some line hap­pens here.

sections.label: India’s borders
sections.head: Honey this side, rice that
sections.caption: India’s porous borders
body: Most of India’s chat­ter­ing class, Ajay Shah said, would like elec­tri­fied fences and ma­chine guns on the bor­ders. But bor­ders are long, and like frac­tals they grow longer the closer you look, so fenc­ing and pa­trolling them is very hard. {#fractal}

The in­cen­tive to trade is strong. There is for­est honey on one side and rice on the other, and the nat­u­ral mar­ket lies across the line. Amit Varma broke in to re­call a song about this from the film *Border*. “Anyway, carry on.” {051-J09}
## Wire cut­ters and dy­na­mite

When a fence gets built, Shah said, some­one uses a wire cut­ter to cut a lit­tle gap, and “sud­denly you’re up and run­ning”. Walls fare no bet­ter, Donald Trump’s in­cluded: a grap­pling hook gets you over, and a small charge of dy­na­mite will blow a hole in one. {#dynamite}

Sealing ef­forts, he ar­gued, con­tain an el­e­ment of pos­tur­ing by par­ties keen to show their base that they are polic­ing the bor­ders. “Realistically, it is not pos­si­ble to seal off the bor­der.” {051-C04}

~ Shah would rather am­plify the half-open ar­range­ments India al­ready has: a free move­ment zone on the Burma bor­der near Nagaland, eight bor­der haats with Bangladesh and an easy bor­der with Nepal.

quote.text: So walls don’t mean much, fences don’t mean much.

sections.label: The European model
sections.head: Old enemies, no checkpoints
sections.caption: Europe’s open borders
body: “To every na­tion­al­ist in India,” Ajay Shah said, “I’d like to say you ain’t seen any­thing yet.” For the fe­roc­ity, ha­tred and cru­elty of na­tion­al­ism, Europe “gets gold medals ga­lore”. {051-J04}

Germany in­vaded France in 1870 and again in 1914, and in­vaded and partly oc­cu­pied it in 1940. {#germany} Out of the ashes of the Second World War came what Shah called one of the great civil­is­ing projects of the world, the European Union.

Today peo­ple who live in France get into a car, drive across the bor­der with­out iden­tity pa­pers or check­points and hold jobs in Germany, not as im­mi­grants but as “a first class par­tic­i­pant” of the Union. {#papers}
The state, Shah said, should add value, as a crim­i­nal jus­tice sys­tem does by pre­vent­ing vi­o­lence, but stay out of “the nat­u­ral en­gage­ments of the peo­ple”. {051-C05}
## Neither French nor German
Near a bor­der peo­ple speak each other’s lan­guages, Shah said, as on the Gujarat–Maharashtra bor­der. At the French–German bor­der, the cul­ture is nei­ther French nor German but a hy­brid of both.

~ The same logic ex­plains a gap in the data, Shah added. The grav­ity model pre­dicts trade far above the real fig­ure in South Asia, where na­tion states have dis­torted the nat­u­ral flow. {051-C08}

quote.text: So at the French German bor­der there is ac­tu­ally nei­ther French nor German cul­ture. There is a hy­brid French German cul­ture.

sections.label: The expanding circle
sections.head: Widening the circle
sections.caption: the expanding circle
body: Amit Varma took his frame from the philoso­pher W. E. H. Lecky, who, he said, wrote *History of European Morals* in 1899. Its the­sis was the ex­pand­ing cir­cle. {051-R08}

In small pre­his­toric tribes, per­haps only the im­me­di­ate fam­ily was wor­thy of moral con­sid­er­a­tion. The cir­cle widened to the tribe, the town, the na­tion, to women and to other races, and Lecky saw it as des­tined to in­clude all of hu­man­ity.
Peter Singer went fur­ther, Varma said, ar­gu­ing that it would ex­pand be­yond hu­mans to in­clude an­i­mals. {#singer}
## Not guar­an­teed

Varma warned against tak­ing the cir­cle for granted, given the po­lar­i­sa­tion and oth­er­ing of re­cent decades. The bar­ri­ers are the lines we draw: this is my coun­try, that is an­other coun­try, and soon “an evil coun­try”. {051-C09}

He does not un­der­stand why “glob­al­ist” has be­come a pe­jo­ra­tive. In sport, he cheers for the way Pep Guardiola’s teams play, from Barcelona to Manchester City, and for Levon Aronian at chess, with no tribal loy­alty. {051-J13}
~ Ajay Shah called it “so up­side down”. People on ei­ther side of a bor­der are each other’s in­ner­most cir­cle, so the line falls through the very cen­tre of it.

quote.text: One of the con­cep­tual bar­ri­ers to this ex­pand­ing cir­cle are the lines with which we have di­vided our­selves.

sections.label: Chosen communities
sections.head: A thousand fans, anywhere
sections.caption: communities of choice
body: Had he been born twenty years ear­lier, Amit Varma said, he would have been a much sad­der per­son. {#twenty}

For most of his­tory, peo­ple lived in com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance: born in a place, a caste or a class, sent to a par­tic­u­lar school, col­lege and of­fice. You mostly met peo­ple like your­self, and could not grow.

The in­ter­net let Varma move to com­mu­ni­ties of choice, built on shared in­ter­ests, val­ues and pas­sions. For cre­ators, he said, Kevin Kelly’s thou­sand true fans can be scat­tered any­where and still make the work vi­able. {051-R10} He often quotes Paul Graham’s line that it is bet­ter to be loved by a few than liked by many. {051-J12}

In media and en­ter­tain­ment, he said, the main­stream is crum­bling, and he counts the na­tion state as an­other main­stream grow­ing less rel­e­vant, though na­tion­al­ism is as­sert­ing it­self across the world.
## Atoms and hugs
Ajay Shah urged cau­tion. There is a death of dis­tance for elec­trons, he said, but “with phys­i­cal goods there is no es­cap­ing the tyranny of dis­tance”. {051-C11}
~ Pots of honey and rice are heavy. And human be­ings need to meet, have chai and touch: no amount of video con­fer­enc­ing, Shah said, can re­place that.

quote.text: I could move away from com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance to com­mu­ni­ties of choice.

sections.label: Divided nations
sections.head: Walls made of words
sections.caption: walls of brick and of words
body: Korea and Germany, Amit Varma said, are what eco­nom­ics and po­lit­i­cal sci­ence rarely get: nat­u­ral ex­per­i­ments. The same peo­ple were di­vided in two, and only one half was al­lowed free­dom. {051-C13}

South Korea and West Germany showed the power of free mar­kets and in­di­vid­ual lib­erty; North Korea and East Germany, the tragic al­ter­na­tive. Varma rec­om­mended a film on the sec­ond, *The Lives of Others*, by a German di­rec­tor whose name he could not pro­nounce. “Florian, if you’re watch­ing, I’m sorry.” {051-J06}
He sees an irony in America, too. Ronald Reagan said “Tear down this wall”; a later Republican pres­i­dent, Donald Trump, wants to build one. {051-J10}
## The rhetoric of di­vi­sion

Walls can also be built with words, Varma warned: rhetoric and ways of see­ing the world can split neigh­bours liv­ing side by side, in India and else­where. Still, re­call­ing Joan Robinson’s line that what­ever you say about India the op­po­site is also true, he saw rea­son for hope.
Ajay Shah asked whether such schisms could over­ride the im­mense gains from trade be­tween two peo­ple about to do busi­ness, be­come friends or be­come lovers. {#lovers}

~ Varma’s an­swer was that the gains from trade need free­dom to flour­ish. Where there are scarci­ties, miss­ing mar­kets and an op­pres­sive state, he said, the schisms ex­press them­selves more. {#scarcity}

quote.text: words, rhetoric, lan­guage, can also build those kinds of metaphor­i­cal walls be­tween the same peo­ple liv­ing side by side
And that to me is the height of civ­i­liza­tion. Saying, yeah, you have your na­tion state, but don’t in­ter­fere in the lives of the peo­ple.

p3.title: Across the line
p3.deck: Four stories from the borderlands, and what each one teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s 2006 cricket tour, and a city of two layers
stories.head: A tale of two Lahores
body: In 2006 Amit Varma spent a few weeks trav­el­ling through Pakistan, fol­low­ing an Indian cricket tour and live-blogging as he went. {#lahore2006}
Lahore sur­prised him. At three in the morn­ing he blogged a pic­ture of kids play­ing cricket out on the street.
You could order food from any­where. And even though it was an Islamic Republic, he said, you could get al­co­hol and recre­ational drugs “super eas­ily”.
Apart from one or two stray in­ci­dents, he met warmth ev­ery­where he went. “I don’t know how much of that Pakistanis would get here,” he said, “but it was won­der­ful.” {#warmth}

What he found were “over­lap­ping Pakistans over there, over­lap­ping Lahores as it were”. One layer was the Punjabiyat that Indians know well, ef­fu­sive and warm, handed down for cen­turies and alive in the kite-flying fes­ti­val. {051-S05}
The other was “a shrill harsh­ness of the Islamic Republic State”, with its rules and laws. The two, he said, co­ex­ist un­easily.

The hard­ened bor­der is it­self fairly new, Varma pointed out. For years after Partition, well into the fifties, the India–Pakistan bor­der was fairly por­ous: peo­ple crossed to visit rel­a­tives and came back. “It worked won­der­fully well.” {#fifties}

~ He set the scene be­side the European Union, where it is un­der­stood that so­ci­ety mat­ters and the state is sub­sidiary, its job the rule of law and a few ba­sics. In India, he said, “it’s sort of the other way around.”
stories.why: A society’s lived cul­ture and its state ide­ol­ogy are sep­a­rate lay­ers. In Lahore the cul­ture had far more in com­mon with India than the state would admit, and the closed bor­der that seems per­ma­nent is a re­cent nor­mal.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Partition interview that turned on itself
stories.head: Present company excepted
body: While re­search­ing her book on Partition, Aanchal Malhotra sat with a Pakistani fam­ily in Lahore or Karachi that had suf­fered through it. They were shar­ing their mem­o­ries with her, Amit Varma re­called.

Then one of them went on a lit­tle bit of a rant: Hindus are this, Hindus are that. Mid-flow, she sud­denly re­alised that Aanchal was sit­ting right there with them. {051-S02} The lady turned to Aanchal and re­as­sured her that she did not mean her.

That made Varma think about the ab­stract and the con­crete. “The line on the map is ab­stract,” he said. People talk­ing, being friends, hav­ing a drink to­gether: “that is con­crete, that human con­nec­tion.” {051-C03}
~ Varma rec­om­mended her book, *Remnants of a Separation*, built from the mem­o­ries of fam­i­lies who lived through Partition.
stories.why: Prejudice sur­vives on ab­strac­tions such as ‘Hindus’ or ‘foreigners’, and fal­ters when the ab­strac­tion be­comes a real per­son across the table. For Varma the human con­nec­tion is real, and the line on the map is the fic­tion.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on a rant that stopped mid-sentence

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s markets at the Bangladesh border
stories.head: Cash only, barter welcome
body: India has built bor­der haats on its bor­der with Bangladesh: con­trolled mar­ket­places where peo­ple from both sides come to­gether to trade. It has built eight, which Ajay Shah called piti­fully small given the size of the bor­der. {#eight}

The rule was that all trans­ac­tions would be con­ducted only in Indian ru­pees. Then the traders from the other side pointed out that they had no Indian ru­pees. Fine, came the reply: barter would do. {051-S04}

Shah called this a healthy thing, a step for­ward from “some Stalinist po­si­tion of say­ing we will cut you off com­pletely”. On the Burma bor­der near Nagaland there is a free move­ment zone with a cer­tain amount of give, and the Nepal bor­der is flex­i­ble and friendly. {#nepal}
~ He wants such ar­range­ments am­pli­fied, be­cause both coun­tries reap the gains from trade.

quote.text: it is a very harm­ful thing for peo­ple to ac­tu­ally be cut off from each other.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the border haats

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s advice to a student learning English
stories.head: Lessons in a borrowed tongue
body: A par­tic­i­pant in Amit Varma’s writ­ing course told him that her first lan­guage was Hindi, that she was only now learn­ing English, and asked what she should do.

Varma pointed her to Agota Kristof, a Hungarian writer who had to flee to France dur­ing the tu­mul­tuous twen­ti­eth cen­tury and learned French as an adult. In it she wrote *The Notebook Trilogy*, which he called a mas­ter­piece. {051-R13}

The stu­dent bought the books. Later she told Varma she had sat down with them and copied the sen­tences out her­self, “to sort of get the rhythm of the lan­guage, get a feel of the lan­guage, in­ter­nal­ize it.” {051-S06}
~ Some writ­ers who come to a lan­guage late, like Nabokov, revel in it floridly. Kristof, Varma said, stripped both the lan­guage and the nar­ra­tive down to their ba­sics.
stories.why: Copying a stylist’s sen­tences is an old way to ab­sorb how a lan­guage moves. Spare prose by a writer who also came to the lan­guage late makes a good model, and Varma found its power sur­vived even in English trans­la­tion.
stories.postscript: Varma first heard of Kristof when Jhumpa Lahiri, who had learned Italian as an adult, named her as a model to Tyler Cowen. {#lahiri}

quiz.q: What determines trade between two countries in the economists’ gravity model?
quiz.a: Their GDPs mul­ti­plied, di­vided by the square of the dis­tance be­tween them.

quiz.q: Why did India’s border haats with Bangladesh end up accepting barter?
quiz.a: Traders across the bor­der said they had no Indian ru­pees to pay with.

quiz.q: Whose imagined maps are drawn by which souring agent a region cooks with?
quiz.a: The food writer Pushpesh Pant’s: tamarind or kokum, jack­fruit or lime.

quiz.q: Where does the gravity model most overpredict trade, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: South Asia, where na­tion states have choked trade be­tween near neigh­bours.

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma say the internet let him move towards?
quiz.a: From com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance to com­mu­ni­ties of choice, built on shared in­ter­ests and val­ues.

quiz.q: Which two divided nations did Varma call natural experiments in freedom?
quiz.a: Korea and Germany: the same peo­ple split, only one half given free­dom.

glossary.def: A mar­ket; at the India–Bangladesh bor­der, a con­trolled one for both sides
Trade pre­dicted from two economies’ size and their dis­tance apart
Economists’ long­ing for the ex­act­ness of physics, which Shah ad­mits
Shared Punjabi cul­ture, ef­fu­sive and warm, found on both sides
A mixed dish; Varma’s image for a blended shared cul­ture
A shape that grows longer the closer you look at it

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 51. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Ronald Reagan (Michael Evans, public domain); Mexico–United States border (Sgt. 1st Class Gordon Hyde, public domain); Isaac Newton (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Peter Singer (Ula Zarosa, CC BY 2.0); William Edward Hartpole Lecky (Julia Margaret Cameron (1815-1879), public domain); Kevin Kelly (Cmichel67, CC BY-SA 4.0); Saadat Hasan Manto (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Ágota Kristóf (Pan Peter12, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A re­mark­able con­ver­sa­tion in which Pushpesh Pant urges Indians to ex­plore their own country’s food di­ver­sity, shar­ing the imag­ined maps in his head (re­gions mapped by their sour­ing agent) and how ‘clas­si­cally Indian’ in­gre­di­ents came from out­side.

shelf.title: Arati Kumar-Rao Took a One-Way Ticket (Episode 383 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It looks at people’s lived con­nec­tion with the land they in­habit, which sits in con­trast to the po­lit­i­cal maps taught in ge­og­ra­phy class.

shelf.title: Marginlands: Indian Landscapes on the Brink
shelf.creator: Arati Kumar-Rao
shelf.why: It is a com­pan­ion to the lived, land-based way of see­ing ge­og­ra­phy that Amit holds up against lines on maps.

shelf.title: Toba Tek Singh
shelf.creator: Saadat Hasan Manto
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great short story about one of the most tragic bor­ders, and one that is close to home.

shelf.title: Memories and Things (Episode 195 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Aanchal Malhotra on mem­o­ries and the things that carry them: the con­ver­sa­tion where Amit began think­ing se­ri­ously about ab­stract cat­e­gories ver­sus con­crete human con­nec­tion, and that gave him his ‘Chinese whis­pers all the way down’ view of mem­ory.

shelf.title: Remnants of a Separation
shelf.creator: Aanchal Malhotra
shelf.why: Aanchal Malhotra’s book on Partition, built from the mem­o­ries of fam­i­lies who lived through it; pre­par­ing to in­ter­view her taught Amit how mem­ory re­shapes it­self every time it is re­called.

shelf.title: A Trade Deficit With a Babysitter
shelf.creator: Tim Harford
shelf.why: Harford al­ways pays his babysit­ter and she buys noth­ing from him, yet both are bet­ter off: a neat de­mo­li­tion of panic about bi­lat­eral trade deficits and of the mis­lead­ing word ‘deficit’.

shelf.title: History of European Morals
shelf.creator: WEH Lecky
shelf.why: The source of the ‘ex­pand­ing circle’: through his­tory we ex­tend moral con­sid­er­a­tion from fam­ily to tribe to na­tion and be­yond.

shelf.title: The Expanding Circle
shelf.creator: Peter Singer
shelf.why: Singer’s ar­gu­ment that our moral cir­cle keeps widen­ing and will one day in­clude an­i­mals.

shelf.title: 1000 True Fans
shelf.creator: Kevin Kelly
shelf.why: Kevin Kelly’s ar­gu­ment that cre­ators don’t need scale: a thou­sand true fans pay­ing $100 a year is a liv­ing, wher­ever in the world they are.

shelf.title: The Lives of Others
shelf.creator: Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck
shelf.why: A debut film about sur­veil­lance in di­vided Germany, about watch­ing and being watched and how that changes both sides; Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece and one of the finest debut films he has seen.

shelf.title: Jhumpa Lahiri on Writing, Translation, and Crossing Between Cultures (Episode 17 of Conversations With Tyler)
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: A great in­ter­view in which Jhumpa Lahiri dis­cusses learn­ing Italian from scratch as an adult and writ­ing a book in it, and names Agota Kristof as a model.

shelf.title: The Notebook Trilogy
shelf.creator: Agota Kristof
shelf.why: Agota Kristof fled Hungary, learned French as an adult and wrote these nov­els in it, strip­ping prose and nar­ra­tive to the bone with enor­mous power.

laughs.text: Ajay’s open­ing para­ble: the Lord holds an ac­count­abil­ity ses­sion and asks every pro­fes­sion to prove it has added value. The econ­o­mists in­clude the grav­ity model on their résumé. The Lord replies, ‘Gravity? But that’s what the physi­cists do.’ Ajay adds that econ­o­mists ‘all suf­fer from physics envy, just like me,’ and that, ‘being im­pe­ri­al­ists,’ they then claimed a gen­eral grav­ity law in the af­fairs of men.

Amit tells Ajay he is ‘an econ­o­mist who has a poet’s heart.’ Later, after Ajay’s line about a bor­der putting ‘a line through their heart,’ Amit adds: ‘In this field right now, there is no bor­der be­tween econ­o­mists and poets.’
Ajay to Indian na­tion­al­ists: ‘you ain’t seen any­thing yet. If you think of the fe­roc­ity, the ha­tred, the cru­elty of na­tion­al­ism, Europe gets gold medals ga­lore.’
After ex­plain­ing that fully mil­i­tarised bor­ders re­ally can split one peo­ple into two, Ajay dead­pans: ‘Not that I’m rec­om­mend­ing this to any­body who’s watch­ing the show.’
Amit strug­gling with the di­rec­tor of The Lives of Others: ‘Forgive me for the pro­nun­ci­a­tion. Florian, if you’re watch­ing, I’m sorry.’

John le Carré: Ajay says we imag­ine bor­ders as a one-kilometre de­mil­i­tarised zone with men hold­ing ma­chine guns, ‘like all of us have read in John le Carré nov­els.’ In re­al­ity a bor­der is usu­ally just a field.

Ronald Reagan’s ‘tear down this wall’ speech, which Amit sets against Donald Trump’s prom­ise to build a wall on the Mexican bor­der: from one Republican pres­i­dent say­ing ‘Tear down this wall’ to an­other who wants to build one.

Sport be­yond bor­ders: Amit says he cheers for the way Pep Guardiola’s teams play, ‘from Barcelona to Manchester City,’ with­out any tribal loy­alty to those clubs, and for Levon Aronian when he plays chess.
